subject: Community N-Mixture “DRY” Model using an over-dispersed dataset

messages.author: 16c477086ae9b88c
messages.subject: Community N-Mixture “DRY” Model using an over-dispersed dataset
parts:
Hi Everyone,

 

I have a dataset of three replicates of point count data from 23 island sites (comprising a total 90 points) and 1 mainland site comprised of 60 points along two dozen transects where it was feasible to safely clamber out of the boat. The mainland site data is combined together, resulting in a dataset where the sum of observed counts per site ranges from 12 individuals on smallest island to 1750 individuals on mainland.

 

This dataset works nicely using a community occupancy model with PX-DA and habitat covariates. In the occupancy model, the range of species richness data is narrower by a degree of magnitude (6 species on smallest island to 75 on ML); however, running an adaptation of the DRY model on count data results in a clear over-estimation of derived abundance on the smallest islands. 

 

I think probably the issue is due to Bayesian shrinkage wherein the tiny islands (<1 hectare comprised of just a point or two) are borrowing strength from the 5500 hectare mainland with its counts compiled from 60 points.

 

In addition to logArea, the other less important habitat parameter, distance from mainland, has a similar effect on some of the island abundance estimates. The highly populated mainland site is rather close to itself, while the most distant islands lie 1000 metres away.

 

The abundance dataset is clearly over-dispersed, which necessitates a negative-binomial distribution rather than the usual Poisson for the abundance process in the DRY model. From what I gather (AHM Ch. 7, p. 337), modelling for dnegbin is not such a straightforward process using jags.   

 

Is there a way to set up the model to account for negative-binomial data, and would this possibly result in more realistic abundance estimates in the smaller and more distant sites?

 

Grateful for any suggestions.

 

Cheers,

 

Greg

messages.author: 4b85f40a0f87fa84
messages.subject: Re: Community N-Mixture “DRY” Model using an over-dispersed dataset
parts:
Hi Greg,
you can find an example for the Poisson-Gamma mixture implementation of the negative binomial distribution in JAGS in the Supplementary Material to our community distance sampling paper:
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12518/full\
I am pretty sure we followed an example in the WinBUGS manual.
The piece of code for the negative binomial abundance model is this (looping over j sites and s species):
     	    N[j,s]~dpois(lambda.star[j,s])  
	    lambda.star[j,s]<-lambda[j,s]*rho.N[j,s]  
	    rho.N[j,s]~dgamma(r.N,r.N)

r.N~dunif(0,100)
Lambda[j,s] can modeled on the log scale as a function of covariates.
Best
Rahel

messages.author: 16c477086ae9b88c
messages.subject: Re: Community N-Mixture “DRY” Model using an over-dispersed dataset
parts:
Hi Rahel,

Thanks a lot for your advice. I enjoyed rediscovering your paper.

I ran the model using the Poisson/gamma correction to the overdispersion, but the results are quite similar to previous analyses. Total abundance is estimated at >9000 individuals vs. 3,433 individual raw counts (high-end, as some individuals are double or triple counted). The abundance on smaller islands is impossible. 

The next step, I think, is to just reorganise the dataset with a more realistic definition of sites. Rather than one overwhelming mainland site, I will break the mainland count data down into its constituent 24 locations, each with 2-3 points. Habitat covariates for mainland will be dealt with by using the same values for each site (5500 hectares (3.7 on log scale) and a small non-zero value for distance from mainland). The detection error-corrected abundance z-matrix can then be produced, and the mainland abundance combined by simply summing up abundance of each species at each mainland site. Then perform a common sense goodness-of-fit analysis. 

Before running the analysis with this re-defined dataset, I will look at how the raw count data is distributed and quickly do model averaging to see if any covariates should be added to the ecological process model (unlikely to change, but should be thorough in any case). I will then run the model separately with the Poisson and Poisson/gamma distributions to see how they differ. Then choose which result to utilise. 

Any other thoughts?

Best regards,

Greg
